newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals - business slow as summer slump hits.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals - business slow as summer slump hits.

text.p: Trading in the minor metals markets continued to slow this week, as the summer seasonal slowdown bit into activity, traders said.
There was little significant price movement or interest in most metals, they said.
"It is holiday time, and half the world is shut," one said.
However, there were pockets of business in markets such as cobalt and cadmium at times, which kept traders on their toes.
"It is July and it is quiet, but we have also been busy which is a bit of a contradiction," one cobalt trader said.
But that was the exception, as the general tone of the market was very low-key, and expected to remain so as summer plant closures intensify in Continental Europe next month.
"There is no real change in conditions, you just have to sit it out and wait for the fourth quarter,' another trader noted.
Cobalt was seeing some interest for very prompt Russian metal, which traders said was thin on the ground and due to the lack of fresh shipments from Russia.

Although producer Norilsk is freely shipping copper and nickel, now that the summer seasonal floods at the port have abated, it is holding back on cobalt. This is because there is a perception that recent prices have been pushed artificialy lower.
"I think they feel the price should be nearer $22/lb, so they are just holding off. After all, they are getting cash from sales of copper and nickel," a cobalt trader said.
Cadmium prices were also showing signs of bubbling, with "three-nines-five" sticks trading at the higher end of the current price range.
Some traders said the market has been running short for some time, with prices having been in a long overall downtrend.
Previously, shorts were able to borrow metal to roll forward positions, but that may not be the case in the future, they added.
In antimony, the market was generally seen as slow, and prices were broadly unchanged on balance with opinions mixed on near-term price direction still.
Elsewhere, a similar scenario prevailed in the molybdenum market, which on balance remained unchanged over the last week.
In magnesium, however, upward pressure appeared to be developing, particularly for Chinese metal with offers being pitched at higher levels, traders noted.
"Consumers have run down their stocks, and I see that the producers are raising their prices now," a trader noted.
On Thursday, Belgium-based Hydro Magnesium, part of Norsk Hydro, lifted its European producer price to 5.75 marks a kilo from 5.55.
Vanadium was also edging higher, reflecting reasonable demand from the Far East, while Chinese offers were being pitched at higher levels.
--Martin Hayes,London Newsroom 44 171 542 8080
